add-authzclientcryptoprovider-for-author.texto: WHAT: readLength validates content length against the total input length (`limit`) instead of the number of bytes remaining, and skips bounds checking entirely for short-form lengths. WHY: This accepts malformed lengths that exceed the current structure and can reject valid nested lengths, producing incorrect parsing or misleading error messages. HOW: Compute the remaining bytes (`limit - count`) and enforce `length <= remaining` uniformly for both short-form and long-form length encodings.

WHAT: detectProvider selects the first provider after sorting by descending order, but DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all declare order 200. WHY: If more than one server crypto provider is present on the classpath, selection falls back to ServiceLoader iteration order, which is non-deterministic and can silently switch crypto behavior between JVM starts. HOW: Assign distinct order values to each concrete server provider or add a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g., class name) after the order comparison.

add-comprehensive-email-validation-for-b.texto: WHAT: BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write update of match_count and last_match_at without locking. WHY: Two concurrent signups for the same blocked email both read the same match_count, each increment it locally, and one save overwrites the other, so block statistics are under-counted and last_match_at is clobbered. HOW: Use atomic increment, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1', last_match_at: Time.zone.now)` to fetch/update in one statement, or wrap the read-increment-save in optimistic locking/transaction with SELECT FOR UPDATE.

WHAT: record.save return value is ignored in should_block?. WHY: If the update fails (record deleted between read and write, constraint violation, DB error), the match_count/last_match_at stats are silently lost and the method still returns the block decision. HOW: Use record.save! to surface persistence failures, or check save result and handle failure explicitly.

BlockedEmail stores and matches emails case-sensitively. Email addresses are case-insensitive, so a user can bypass a block by submitting a differently-cased variant (e.g., Bad@Example.com vs bad@example.com), and the case-sensitive unique index allows duplicate blocked records for the same address. Normalize the email with Email.downcase (or a full downcase) before save and lookup, and make the index/lookup case-insensitive.

add-groups-resource-type-and-scopes-to-a.texto: canManage() evaluates VIEW as sufficient for management access. WHAT: The manage check falls back to hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE) instead of requiring MANAGE. WHY: An administrator granted only the 'view' scope on Groups will be treated as having 'manage' permission, allowing group modifications that should require the manage scope. HOW: Change to hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE).

canMapRoles no longer honors user-level manage permission. WHAT: The early return changed from if (canManage(user)) to if (root.hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS)), dropping the V2 authz manage check for the specific user and the group-chain fallback path for role mapping. WHY: A fine-grained admin with manage permission on a specific user (but without the global MANAGE_USERS role) loses the ability to map roles to that user, breaking the V2 permission model. HOW: Restore the canManage(user) short-circuit or add the equivalent hasPermission(user, MANAGE) / canManageByGroup(user) check.

canManageGroupMembership no longer honors user-level manage permission. WHAT: The early return changed from if (canManage(user)) to if (root.hasOneAdminRole(MANAGE_USERS)). WHY: A fine-grained admin with manage permission on a specific user (but no global MANAGE_USERS role) can no longer manage that user's group membership under V2. HOW: Restore canManage(user) as the short-circuit or add the equivalent user-level manage/group-chain check.

searchForUser no longer filters results through usersEvaluator.canView. WHAT: The .filter(usersEvaluator::canView) call and the guard that limited group-ids to non-global viewers were removed. WHY: If toRepresentation does not re-apply per-user authorization, callers with only group-scoped view permission may receive users they are not authorized to see. HOW: Verify toRepresentation applies canView per user, or restore the filter in searchForUser.

searchForUser no longer filters results through usersEvaluator.canView. WHAT: The filter and the canView guard around group-ids were removed. WHY: If toRepresentation does not re-apply per-user authorization, brute-force user search results may include users the caller is not authorized to view. HOW: Verify downstream filtering in toRepresentation or restore the usersEvaluator::canView filter.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission performs an authorization evaluation for every group resource. WHAT: findByType iterates all group resources and runs hasPermission for each. WHY: User search and group listing become O(N) in the number of groups with an authz evaluation per group, which is a material slowdown for realms with many groups. HOW: Use a single permission evaluation against the resource type or cache the granted group set per request.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission iterates all group resources and evaluates permissions per resource. WHAT: findByType over type 'Group' with a hasPermission callback for each group. WHY: Listing/searching users when only group-scoped view is present triggers an authz evaluation per group, causing O(N) growth. HOW: Consider evaluating the all-groups type resource once or batching the evaluation.

add-rolling-updates-feature-flag-and-com.texto: WHAT: The recreate-upgrade exit code was changed from 4 to 3, and the new feature-disabled condition now uses 4. WHY: This reassigns a previously documented exit-code contract, so existing scripts and automation that treated exit code 4 as 'recreate upgrade required' will now misinterpret recreate-upgrade results as 'feature disabled'. HOW: Keep RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE at 4 and assign FEATURE_DISABLED a different unused value (e.g., 5), or document the breaking change explicitly if backward compatibility is intentionally abandoned.

advanced-date-override-handling-and-time.texto: WHAT: When a slot falls within a date override, checkIfIsAvailable returns true before verifying the user's busy bookings. WHY: Existing meetings on overridden days are ignored, so slots overlapping real bookings can be shown as available. HOW: Remove the early return true when dateOverrideExist is set and fall through to the busy.every(...) check; only bypass the normal working-hours check, not the busy check.

WHAT: The working-hours end boundary is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime. WHY: Slots that begin before the working-day ends but extend past it pass the availability check, allowing bookings outside working hours. HOW: Change the end calculation to slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute().

WHAT: The working-hours check uses .find to return true when the slot is outside any single range. WHY: With multiple ranges on the same day (e.g., 9:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00), a valid 10:00 slot is rejected because it is outside the 14:00–17:00 range. HOW: Use .some to verify the slot falls inside at least one range for that day, returning false only when no range contains it.

WHAT: The zero-length override guard compares two Dayjs objects with ===, which is always false because it tests object identity, not value. WHY: A date override with equal start and end times is treated as an available window instead of being rejected as unavailable. HOW: Use .isSame() to compare the two Dayjs values.

When a slot falls on a day with a date override, checkIfIsAvailable returns true at line 134 before the busy.every check. A host who has a date override but also a conflicting booking will still be shown as available, allowing double-booking. Continue to the busy check instead of returning early.

The working-hours end boundary is computed from slotStartTime on line 143 instead of slotEndTime. A slot that starts inside working hours but extends past the host's availability end will never be rejected, allowing bookings that exceed the configured hours.

The working-hours guard uses workingHours.find and returns false when the slot is outside the first matching range. With multiple ranges for the same day (e.g., split availability), a slot that falls inside a later range is incorrectly rejected. Reject only when the slot is outside every range for that day.

The zero-length override guard compares two dayjs objects with === on line 115, which tests object identity and is always false. A zero-length override intended to block the whole day will not mark slots unavailable. Compare formatted values or timestamps instead.

advanced-query-processing-architecture-g.texto: runSplitQuery re-interpolates queries that were already interpolated by runShardSplitQuery. When splitQueriesByStreamShard delegates to runSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), applyTemplateVariables is invoked twice on the same targets, causing ad-hoc filters to be appended multiple times and potentially mangling already-replaced template values. Either skip interpolation when the caller has already interpolated, or change runShardSplitQuery to delegate to a shared splitter that does not re-apply template variables.

runSplitQuery double-interpolates queries when invoked from runShardSplitQuery. Because runShardSplitQuery already calls applyTemplateVariables on line 52, runSplitQuery re-applies template variables and ad-hoc filters on the already-interpolated sub-request targets, which duplicates ad-hoc filter labels in the Loki expression. Consider skipping interpolation in runSplitQuery when the incoming request/targets are already interpolated, or moving the single interpolation point higher so it happens only once per query.

advanced-sql-analytics-framework-grafana.texto: WHAT: `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false regardless of the `sqlExpressions` feature flag. WHY: It negates `IsEnabledGlobally` and then unconditionally returns false, so enabling the feature flag cannot turn SQL expressions on, breaking the flag's contract. HOW: Return the flag value directly (`return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`) if conditional gating is intended, or return `false` explicitly if the intent is to permanently disable.

WHAT: The new SQL-expression gate is only applied inside `ReadQuery` and not in the legacy `buildCMDNode` path at nodes.go:160. WHY: When `FlagExpressionParser` is disabled, `buildCMDNode` calls `UnmarshalSQLCommand` directly, bypassing `enableSqlExpressions`; although the stub DB currently makes this fail with a different error, the disable is inconsistent and could be circumvented if the stub is replaced or the error is mishandled. HOW: Move the enablement check into `NewSQLCommand` or `UnmarshalSQLCommand` so all construction paths enforce the same gate.

WHAT: `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false regardless of the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle. WHY: The toggle is documented to enable SQL/DuckDB expressions, but the helper negates `IsEnabledGlobally` and then unconditionally returns false, so the flag cannot enable the feature and the check is dead code. HOW: Return `h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` directly, or remove the toggle check if the intent is a permanent hard-disable.

async-import-of-the-appstore-packages-ca.texto: The credentials.forEach(async (credential) => {...}) callback is not awaited, so apiDeletes may be empty or incomplete when Promise.all(apiDeletes) runs and the function can return before recurring calendar deletions finish. Replace forEach with a for...of loop and await each deletion, or collect the returned promises into an array and await Promise.all.

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) fires async calendar/video deletions without awaiting them; the router continues to sendRequestRescheduleEmail and beyond before deletions complete, risking lost cleanup and uncaught errors. Replace forEach with for...of and await each operation, or gather promises into Promise.all.

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) runs the async getCalendar/deleteEvent callbacks in the background; the surrounding try/catch cannot catch their errors and the function may return before cleanup finishes. Convert to a for...of loop with await or Promise.all over an array of promises.

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...}) runs the async getCalendar/deleteEvent callbacks in the background; the surrounding try/catch cannot catch their errors and the function may return before cleanup finishes. Convert to a for...of loop with await or Promise.all over an array of promises.

The `.forEach(async ...)` pattern pushes promises into `apiDeletes`/`integrationsToDelete` from an async callback, so the subsequent `Promise.all` may execute before the pushes complete, missing the intended deletions. Collect the promises with `map` (or `for...of` with `await`) instead of `forEach(async ...)` so all pushes are guaranteed to have happened before `Promise.all` runs.

Same introduced regression as in handleCancelBooking.ts: promises are pushed into `apiDeletes`/`integrationsToDelete` inside an async `.forEach` callback in the reschedule and bookings routers, so the following `Promise.all` may run before the pushes happen. Replace `forEach(async ...)` with `map`/`for...of` to ensure pushes complete before awaiting.

authzservice-improve-authz-caching-grafa.texto: WHAT: permissionCacheUsage is incremented with cache_hit="false" both when the permission cache is actually absent and when the cache is present but checkPermission returns denied. WHY: This makes the metric unable to distinguish a real cache miss from a cached-but-denied permission, changing the semantic meaning of the cache_hit label. HOW: Only increment permissionCacheUsage with cache_hit="false" when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns an error (cache miss); do not increment it when cached permissions exist and simply deny the request.

Stale denial cache can deny access after permissions are granted. Check() consults permDenialCache before permCache and sets it on every DB denial, but never invalidates it when permissions change or when permCache is refreshed. Because the two caches are independent keys with the same 30s TTL, a fresh permission entry in permCache can be overridden by a stale denial entry for up to 30 seconds. Either invalidate the matching denial entry when permissions are refreshed, check permCache before the denial cache, or use a much shorter TTL for denials.

permissionCacheUsage metric with cache_hit="false" is incremented both when the permission cache entry is absent and when the entry exists but the requested resource is not in the cached scope map. This conflates a true cache miss with a cache hit that results in a permission denial, making the cache hit rate metric misleading. Emit cache_hit="true" when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a map (the cache entry was found), and only emit "false" on an actual cache miss/error.

comprehensive-workflow-reminder-manageme.texto: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async but are invoked inside .forEach without await, so the cancelled: true update / row deletion and the external API calls may not commit before the handler returns and errors are silently swallowed. Replace forEach with a Promise.all(map(...)) and await it so cancellation state is guaranteed to persist before responding.

deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true) cancels the SendGrid scheduled send but never deletes or marks the original rescheduled booking's workflowReminder row, leaving orphaned scheduled reminders in the database. Either delete the row here or mark it cancelled so the cron job can clean it up.

The remindersToCancel query filters only by cancelled: true and scheduledDate, without restricting to method: EMAIL or referenceId: { not: null }. If an SMS or reference-less row is ever flagged cancelled, the SendGrid request will fail because batch_id is missing or wrong. Add method and referenceId filters to match the SendGrid cancellation path.

scheduledReminders.forEach launches all deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder promises concurrently without awaiting or limiting concurrency, creating unbounded fan-out to SendGrid/Twilio when a workflow has many scheduled reminders. Use Promise.all with a concurrency limit (e.g., p-map) or sequential await to avoid overwhelming the downstream APIs.

Async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` calls are fire-and-forget inside `.forEach` and are excluded from `Promise.all`; the previous code awaited the Prisma deletes. This means DB cancellation updates may not complete before the response and errors become unhandled promise rejections. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` them.

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)` cancels the SendGrid scheduled send but returns without deleting or marking the workflow-reminder row, so the original rescheduled booking keeps stale scheduled email reminders in the database. Also, the `try/catch` around `.forEach` cannot catch rejections from async functions that are not awaited. Either delete the row after cancelling or mark it `cancelled: true`, and await the returned promises in the try/catch.

Async `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` calls are fired inside `.forEach` without `await`; the old code collected `PrismaPromise` deletes and awaited them. DB cancellation updates are no longer guaranteed to complete before the TRPC response and errors are swallowed. Collect and await the returned promises.

Reminder cancellations are launched asynchronously without awaiting, and then the workflow is immediately cascade-deleted. The in-flight DB updates/SendGrid cancels can race with the cascade delete and failures are swallowed. Await the cancellation promises before deleting the workflow.

The edit-step path uses `.forEach(async (reminder) => { ... })` but never awaits the resulting promises, so DB cancellations/updates are fire-and-forget and errors are swallowed. Replace with a `for...of` loop or collect promises and `await Promise.all`.

The entire cancellation loop is wrapped in a single `try/catch`. If one SendGrid `cancel` request fails, the loop exits and all remaining cancelled reminders are skipped (and previously collected delete promises are not awaited). Handle each reminder individually or use `Promise.allSettled` so one failure does not abort the batch.

`remindersToCancel` queries `WorkflowReminder` by the new nullable `cancelled` column and `scheduledDate`, but there is no index on either field. As the table grows this cron query will perform a full table scan. Add a composite index such as `@@index([cancelled, scheduledDate])`.

database-performance-optimizations-grafa.texto: Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with a nil err key. This spams the error log and can trigger false alerts for expected behavior. Change these log lines to Debug or Info level and remove the err key when err is known to be nil.

The cleanup ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which is not mentioned in the PR intent and causes the cleanup job to run 10 times more frequently. Revert this to the original 10-minute interval unless the frequency change was intentional and documented.

WHAT: deleteByIDs builds the SQLite inline ID list by repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation inside a loop. WHY: For batch sizes above the 999 SQLite parameter threshold (e.g., the 32767-ID test case), this is O(n²) in string reallocations and allocates several gigabytes of intermediate strings, causing a severe slowdown in the cleanup job. HOW: Build the list with strings.Builder or pre-allocate a []string and strings.Join it.

WHAT: deleteByIDs binds IDs as ? parameters for non-SQLite databases without any batch-size guard or inline fallback. WHY: MySQL supports at most 65535 placeholders per statement and PostgreSQL at most 32767; a configured cleanup batch size above that limit will cause the DELETE to fail, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE worked regardless of batch size. HOW: Apply a dialect-specific placeholder limit and fall back to inline IDs or smaller sub-batches when the limit is exceeded.

enhanced-pagination-performance-for-high.texto: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil directly on the sort-key attribute. For audit logs the key is 'datetime', so getattr returns a datetime object and math.floor raises TypeError, crashing every paginated response. Reuse the DateTimePaginator timestamp conversion or implement datetime-aware key extraction.

BasePaginator.get_result now allows negative offsets for is_prev cursors, passing them unchanged to queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django negative slicing returns the tail of the queryset rather than rows before the cursor, breaking reverse-pagination semantics and producing wrong page contents.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result explicitly enables negative-offset slicing and then compares len(results) against a negative offset at line 891, so the extra-row trimming branch is almost never selected and the returned page/cursor is incorrect.

Negative Django slicing (queryset[offset:stop] with offset<0) generates SQL that counts the full result set and skips to the end. An admin can supply a large-magnitude negative offset against the audit-log table, causing an expensive sequential scan and skip without any upper bound on offset magnitude.

WHAT: OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value instead of converting it back to a datetime. WHY: For the audit-logs endpoint the paginator is used with order_by='-datetime', so build_queryset compares the integer cursor value against the datetime column (e.g., auditlogentry.datetime >= 1697800000), causing a database type mismatch or wrong pagination boundary. HOW: Convert cursor.value back to a datetime, mirroring DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor.

feat-add-calendar-cache-status-and-actio.texto: Passing an empty data object to updateManyByCredentialId does not update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt because Prisma treats data: {} as a no-op and skips @updatedAt. The comment says the intent is to update updatedAt for all calendars under the credential, but the call fails to do so. Pass { updatedAt: new Date() } as the data argument so the timestamp is actually refreshed.

Passing an empty data object to updateManyByCredentialId does not update any fields, so the @updatedAt field on SelectedCalendar is never refreshed. The cache-status logic intends to record when calendars were last synced, but this call is a no-op. Pass an explicit updatedAt value (e.g., { updatedAt: new Date() }) or another real field change so Prisma applies the timestamp.

The authorization check only matches credential.userId, ignoring team-owned credentials. Team/delegation credentials can have userId null, so legitimate members are denied and the boundary is inconsistent with the existing credentials.delete handler, which accepts teamId and delegates to handleDeleteCredential. Add teamId to the input and verify the caller belongs to the credential's team before deleting cache.

feat-upsampling-support-upsampled-error-.texto:
WHAT: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only matches the literal `count()` after lowercasing and stripping, so it misses other valid ways a count aggregate can appear in the y-axis list (e.g. aliased `count() as total`, parentheses variations, or whitespace inside parentheses).
WHY: Queries that the endpoint should convert to `upsampled_count()` will remain as plain `count()`, silently returning unweighted counts for allowlisted projects and breaking the upsampling contract.
HOW: Use the existing search/equation parser to normalize each y-axis expression, or match against the parsed function name rather than the raw string, so any alias or canonical form of `count()` is transformed.

WHAT: `_is_error_focused_query` classifies a Discover query as error-focused whenever the raw query string contains the substring `event.type:error`.
WHY: Negated or compound queries such as `!event.type:error` still contain the substring, so the upsampling transform is incorrectly applied to queries that are not focused on errors, producing weighted counts for transactions or default events.
HOW: Parse the query into structured conditions (e.g. via the event search parser) and return true only when an affirmative `event.type:error` condition is present, not a substring match.

WHAT: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` catches broad `Exception` and silently ignores failures, then accepts any truthy `client_sample_rate` (including non-numeric strings) before attempting `float()` inside another swallowing try/except.
WHY: Malformed `error_sampling.client_sample_rate` values in test events go undetected and can leave `sample_rate` unset or set to an unexpected value, making error-upsampling tests unreliable.
HOW: Replace the blanket `except Exception: pass` blocks with targeted handling (e.g. `AttributeError`/`KeyError` and `ValueError`/`TypeError`) and raise or log an assertion when `client_sample_rate` is present but not a valid number.

WHAT: `_is_error_focused_query` treats any Discover query containing the substring `event.type:error` as an error query. WHY: A negated query such as `!event.type:error` still triggers upsampling, causing the endpoint to sum `sample_weight` on data that is explicitly not errors and return incorrect counts. HOW: Parse the query structure (or at least reject leading `!` / `NOT` before the token) instead of doing a raw substring check.

WHAT: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` stores any truthy `client_sample_rate` as `sample_rate` without validating it is a valid rate in `(0, 1]`. WHY: Negative values or values greater than 1 are cast to float and persisted, which produces invalid `sample_weight` values (`1/sample_rate`) and breaks upsampled count semantics in tests and any code paths that reuse this factory data. HOW: Validate `0 < sample_rate <= 1` after the float conversion and skip or raise for out-of-range values; also narrow the swallowed exceptions so programming errors are not masked.

feat-uptime-add-ability-to-use-queues-to.texto: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and join() both shut down the FixedQueuePool, but that pool is created once per ResultsStrategyFactory and reused across strategy instances (result_consumer.py:131-137). After the first partition revocation/rebalance, the shared pool is dead and the offset tracker still holds stale state, so later strategies cannot process messages and may commit offsets for partitions they no longer own. close() should only signal shutdown of its commit thread; join() should block until the queues drain; the pool should only be shut down by the factory's shutdown().

If the decoder raises for a message whose message.value is not a BrokerValue, the exception handler cannot complete any offset, so that partition's commits stall forever. The assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue) is used as control flow after decoder may already have run. Move the BrokerValue extraction/validation before decoder work and complete the offset on any failure path.

get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) for every partition while holding the partition lock, so large offset gaps cause unbounded O(max-min) work and block worker threads from completing offsets. Replace the linear scan with a sorted/heap structure that can find the next contiguous completed offset in O(log n).

OrderedQueueWorker.run() emits a metrics.gauge for every single processed message in the finally block, adding per-message overhead on the hot path. Move queue-depth reporting to poll() or sample it instead of recording it for every work item.

Strategy lifecycle methods shut down the factory-owned FixedQueuePool. close(), terminate(), and join() all call queue_pool.shutdown(), but ResultsStrategyFactory creates the pool once in __init__ and reuses it across create_with_partitions. When Arroyo rebalances and closes/joins the old strategy then creates a new one, the new strategy uses an already-dead pool, and close followed by join causes a double shutdown. The strategy should drain and wait without shutting down the shared pool; factory.shutdown() is the only place that should terminate the pool.

Unbounded queue.Queue and non-blocking submit provide no backpressure, risking memory exhaustion. FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() without maxsize (line 185) and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after putting the item (lines 293-315). If ingestion outpaces processing the queue grows without bound. Raise MessageRejected or bound the queues and block/raise when full so Arroyo pauses the consumer.

Commit loop scans the entire in-flight offset window per partition while holding the partition lock. get_committable_offsets() iterates range(start, max_offset+1) once per second (lines 89-93), so large in-flight windows cause long lock holds and CPU spikes that block submit/complete. Use a sorted structure or track the contiguous completed prefix to find the committable offset in O(log N).

Per-message metrics.gauge adds hot-path overhead. OrderedQueueWorker.run() calls metrics.gauge in the finally block for every processed item (lines 150-156). In a high-throughput consumer this serialization and metrics emission cost per message undercuts the parallelism gains. Move the gauge to poll() or sample it periodically instead of emitting it for every message.

feature-per-topic-unsubscribe-option-in-.texto: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, and the next line dereferences tu.notification_level without a guard. A user who receives an email about a topic they have never opened may have no TopicUser record, so clicking the unsubscribe link raises NoMethodError. Use TopicUser.get or create a record when none exists before reading notification_level.

The unsubscribe action performs a state-mutating save on a GET request without CSRF token or confirmation. Any third-party site can embed a link or image to /t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe and silently change the notification level of a logged-in user. Convert the mutation to a POST/PUT with CSRF protection, or require a signed per-user token in the URL.

WHAT: TopicUser.find_by returns nil when the user has no row for the topic, and line 107 dereferences tu.notification_level without a guard. WHY: A user who receives an email (e.g., via mention or category watch) but has never visited the topic will get a NoMethodError instead of being unsubscribed. HOW: Create or fetch the TopicUser safely, e.g., using TopicUser.change or TopicUser.find_or_initialize_by, before reading or mutating notification_level.
